children: Roche

said its experimental eye drug vamikibart helped patients maintain improvements in vision for a full year in two late-stage clinical trials, potentially offering an alternative to steroid treatments that can cause serious side effects.

The results, presented at the American Academy of Ophthalmology annual meeting in New Orleans, showed that patients receiving the treatment experienced sustained improvements in eyesight and reduced swelling in the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye.

The drug, developed by Roche's Genentech subsidiary, is designed to treat uveitic macular edema, a condition in which inflammation causes fluid to accumulate in the central part of the retina. The swelling can interfere with reading, driving and other activities that require sharp vision.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has accepted Genentech's application for approval, with a decision expected by July 2027. If approved, the treatment could become the first targeted, non-steroid therapy specifically authorized for the condition.
Lasting benefits
The two Phase 3 studies, called MEERKAT and SANDCAT, compared two doses of vamikibart with a sham procedure designed to mimic an injection into the eye without delivering the experimental medication.
Patients initially received treatment every four weeks for up to 16 weeks. Researchers then followed them through one year, providing additional injections when needed.

At 52 weeks, a higher percentage of patients receiving the drug achieved meaningful vision improvements than those in the comparison groups, although Genentech did not provide the exact percentages in its announcement.
Researchers also observed lasting reductions in retinal swelling, an important measure of whether treatment is controlling the underlying disease.
About two-thirds of eligible patients required no additional injections after the initial 16-week treatment period. Most of those who needed further treatment received only one additional injection.
The findings suggest the therapy could offer lasting benefits without requiring frequent visits for eye injections.
Genentech said the drug was generally well tolerated, with relatively few treatment-related eye complications or cases of inflammation inside the eye.
Different approach to eye inflammation
Uveitic macular edema develops when inflammation damages blood vessels in the retina, allowing fluid to leak into the tissue responsible for detailed central vision.
The condition is a leading cause of vision loss among people with uveitis, an inflammatory eye disease that frequently affects working-age adults.

Current treatment often relies on corticosteroids, which reduce inflammation but can cause complications when used repeatedly or over long periods. These include cataracts and increased pressure inside the eye, which can lead to glaucoma.
Vamikibart takes a more targeted approach by blocking interleukin-6, or IL-6, a protein that helps drive inflammation.
By interfering with this inflammatory signal, researchers hope to reduce swelling and protect vision without exposing patients to some of the long-term risks associated with steroids.

"Vamikibart is the first non-steroid targeted therapy to demonstrate meaningful and sustained visual and anatomical improvements in people with UME," said Dr. Nisha Acharya, a professor of ophthalmology at the University of California, San Francisco.
Genentech estimates that approximately 20% of patients with the condition develop sustained blindness within three years of diagnosis, highlighting the need for more effective treatments.
FDA decision expected in July 2027
The new findings build on earlier results presented in October 2025, when both trials were evaluated after 16 weeks of treatment.
The studies measured how many patients gained at least 15 letters on a standard eye chart, an improvement generally considered meaningful for everyday vision.

The latest one-year findings provide additional evidence that the initial benefits can be maintained over time. However, the announcement did not include detailed numerical results or statistical comparisons for the 52-week outcomes, limiting an independent assessment of the size of the benefit.
Genentech has also submitted applications seeking approval in the European Union, China and Japan, where regulators have accepted the filings for review.
The treatment has received orphan drug designation in the United States and Europe, a status intended to encourage development of medicines for rare diseases.
For investors, the clinical results offer Roche an opportunity to expand its eye disease business with a treatment that works differently from existing therapies.
The potential commercial market is relatively specialized because uveitic macular edema is less common than major retinal diseases such as diabetic macular edema and age-related macular degeneration.
Still, a targeted treatment that provides lasting improvements while reducing reliance on steroids could appeal to physicians managing patients with chronic inflammation.
The FDA's decision next July will be a major milestone in determining whether Roche can turn the promising clinical findings into another approved treatment in its ophthalmology portfolio.
